Looking at this problem, I need to figure out the structure of valid coin configurations and count them.

## Setting Up the Recurrence

**Geometry.** The first (bottom) row has $n$ identical coins packed together. Each row above sits in the gaps of the row below: a row of $k$ coins has $k-1$ gaps, and the row above occupies some number $m \leq k-1$ of *consecutive* gaps (to form a continuous block). Each coin in the upper row touches exactly the two adjacent coins below it. So row sizes strictly decrease: $n = a_1 > a_2 > \cdots > a_k \geq 1$.

**Positioning matters.** If row $i$ has $a_i$ coins and row $i{+}1$ has $a_{i+1}$ coins, the upper row can start at any of $a_i - a_{i+1}$ gaps, giving $a_i - a_{i+1}$ distinct horizontal placements.

**Recursion.** Let $f(n) = A(n)$. A configuration with bottom row $n$ is either:
- Just the bottom row alone (1 way), or
- A second row of $m$ coins ($1 \le m \le n-1$) placed in one of $(n-m)$ positions, with any valid $f(m)$-configuration stacked above it.

$$f(n) = 1 + \sum_{m=1}^{n-1} (n-m)\,f(m), \qquad f(1)=1.$$

## Computing Values

| $n$ | $f(n)$ |
|-----|--------|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | $1+1\cdot1=2$ |
| 3 | $1+2\cdot1+1\cdot2=5$ |
| 4 | $1+3\cdot1+2\cdot2+1\cdot5=13$ |
| 5 | $1+4+6+10+13=34$ |
| 6 | $1+5+8+15+26+34=89$ |

These are $1, 2, 5, 13, 34, 89, \ldots = F(1), F(3), F(5), F(7), F(9), F(11), \ldots$

## Proving $f(n) = F(2n-1)$

**Deriving a simpler recurrence.** From $f(n) = 1 + \sum_{m=1}^{n-1}(n-m)f(m)$:

$$f(n)-f(n-1) = f(n-1) + \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} f(m).$$

Applying the same identity to $f(n-1)-f(n-2) = f(n-2)+\sum_{m=1}^{n-3}f(m)$, so $\sum_{m=1}^{n-3}f(m) = f(n-1)-2f(n-2)$. Substituting:

$$f(n)-f(n-1) = f(n-1) + \bigl(f(n-1)-2f(n-2)\bigr) + f(n-2) = 2f(n-1)-f(n-2).$$

$$\boxed{f(n) = 3f(n-1)-f(n-2)}, \quad f(1)=1,\; f(2)=2.$$

**Fibonacci identity.** The Fibonacci numbers $F(1)=F(2)=1$, $F(k)=F(k{-}1)+F(k{-}2)$ satisfy:

$$3F(2n{-}3)-F(2n{-}5) = 2F(2n{-}3)+F(2n{-}4) = F(2n{-}3)+F(2n{-}2)=F(2n{-}1).$$

With $F(1)=1=f(1)$ and $F(3)=2=f(2)$, induction gives $f(n)=F(2n-1)$ for all $n\ge1$.

## Finding the Smallest $n$

Computing Fibonacci numbers:

| $k$ | $F(k)$ |
|-----|--------|
| 17 | 1597 |
| 18 | 2584 |
| 19 | 4181 |
| 20 | 6765 |
| 21 | **10946** |

$$A(10) = F(19) = 4181 < 10^4, \qquad A(11) = F(21) = 10946 > 10^4.$$

## Answer

The smallest $n$ for which $A(n) > 10^4$ is $\boxed{11}$.

Looking at this problem, I need to figure out the structure of valid coin configurations and count them.

## Setting Up the Recurrence

**Geometry.** The first (bottom) row has $n$ identical coins packed together. Each row above sits in the gaps of the row below: a row of $k$ coins has $k-1$ gaps, and the row above occupies some number $m \leq k-1$ of *consecutive* gaps (to form a continuous block). Each coin in the upper row touches exactly the two adjacent coins below it. So row sizes strictly decrease: $n = a_1 > a_2 > \cdots > a_k \geq 1$.

**Positioning matters.** If row $i$ has $a_i$ coins and row $i{+}1$ has $a_{i+1}$ coins, the upper row can start at any of $a_i - a_{i+1}$ gaps, giving $a_i - a_{i+1}$ distinct horizontal placements.

**Recursion.** Let $f(n) = A(n)$. A configuration with bottom row $n$ is either:
- Just the bottom row alone (1 way), or
- A second row of $m$ coins ($1 \le m \le n-1$) placed in one of $(n-m)$ positions, with any valid $f(m)$-configuration stacked above it.

$$f(n) = 1 + \sum_{m=1}^{n-1} (n-m)\,f(m), \qquad f(1)=1.$$

## Computing Values

| $n$ | $f(n)$ |
|-----|--------|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | $1+1\cdot1=2$ |
| 3 | $1+2\cdot1+1\cdot2=5$ |
| 4 | $1+3\cdot1+2\cdot2+1\cdot5=13$ |
| 5 | $1+4+6+10+13=34$ |
| 6 | $1+5+8+15+26+34=89$ |

These are $1, 2, 5, 13, 34, 89, \ldots = F(1), F(3), F(5), F(7), F(9), F(11), \ldots$

## Proving $f(n) = F(2n-1)$

**Deriving a simpler recurrence.** From $f(n) = 1 + \sum_{m=1}^{n-1}(n-m)f(m)$:

$$f(n)-f(n-1) = f(n-1) + \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} f(m).$$

Applying the same identity to $f(n-1)-f(n-2) = f(n-2)+\sum_{m=1}^{n-3}f(m)$, so $\sum_{m=1}^{n-3}f(m) = f(n-1)-2f(n-2)$. Substituting:

$$f(n)-f(n-1) = f(n-1) + \bigl(f(n-1)-2f(n-2)\bigr) + f(n-2) = 2f(n-1)-f(n-2).$$

$$\boxed{f(n) = 3f(n-1)-f(n-2)}, \quad f(1)=1,\; f(2)=2.$$

**Fibonacci identity.** The Fibonacci numbers $F(1)=F(2)=1$, $F(k)=F(k{-}1)+F(k{-}2)$ satisfy:

$$3F(2n{-}3)-F(2n{-}5) = 2F(2n{-}3)+F(2n{-}4) = F(2n{-}3)+F(2n{-}2)=F(2n{-}1).$$

With $F(1)=1=f(1)$ and $F(3)=2=f(2)$, induction gives $f(n)=F(2n-1)$ for all $n\ge1$.

## Finding the Smallest $n$

Computing Fibonacci numbers:

| $k$ | $F(k)$ |
|-----|--------|
| 17 | 1597 |
| 18 | 2584 |
| 19 | 4181 |
| 20 | 6765 |
| 21 | **10946** |

$$A(10) = F(19) = 4181 < 10^4, \qquad A(11) = F(21) = 10946 > 10^4.$$

## Answer

The smallest $n$ for which $A(n) > 10^4$ is $\boxed{11}$.
